meta.title: Neural Networks and Backpropagation
meta.thesis: Neural Networks and Backpropagation is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: An invoice classifier needs to learn from errors by moving credit backward through layers. By the end, they should be able to build or review backpropagation walkthrough for one small neural network, measure validation accuracy improves without exploding gradients, and catch the failure where a hidden layer saturates and stops learning.

modules.title: Layers turn raw inputs into representations
modules.sub: Each layer transforms numbers into features the next layer can use.
modules.summary: A network is a stack of parameterized transformations.
objectives: Describe weights, biases, and activations as learned parts of a function.
Trace a tiny input through two layers.
Explain why shape and dimension matter.

blocks.title: A layer is a learned feature maker

spans.text: Problem anchor: classify a support ticket as urgent from two numbers: sentiment score and account value. A neural network does not store a rule like "if sentiment is low then urgent." It learns weights that combine inputs into intermediate features, then combines those features into a prediction.

For beginners, think of each layer as a small spreadsheet: multiply inputs by weights, add biases, pass the result forward. Deep learning scales this simple pattern to many layers and huge parameter counts.

blocks.analogy: A layer is a lens that reshapes raw numbers so the next lens can see a different pattern.

spans.text: Input x = [negative_sentiment=0.8, account_value=0.6]. Hidden unit A uses weights [1.2, 0.4] and bias -0.5, so its pre-activation is 0.8*1.2 + 0.6*0.4 - 0.5 = 0.70. Hidden unit B uses [-0.3, 1.1] and bias 0.1, producing 0.52. Those hidden numbers become the next layer input.

blocks.title: Layer purpose
blocks.prompt: What do learned weights do in a neural network layer?

options.text: They store the training examples verbatim by design.
They control how input numbers are combined into new representations.
They choose the final train/test split.

blocks.explanation: Weights define the parameterized function the model learns.

modules.title: Activations add bends to the function
modules.sub: Nonlinearities let stacked layers model more than one straight line.
modules.summary: Activations such as ReLU let networks represent complex patterns.
objectives: Apply ReLU to a hidden-unit value.
Recognize dead or saturated activation problems.

blocks.title: Without bends, many layers collapse into one line

spans.text: If every layer only multiplies and adds, stacking layers is still one larger linear transformation. Activations such as ReLU introduce bends: negative values become zero, positive values pass through. Those bends let networks carve more flexible decision regions.

Hidden values [0.70, 0.52] stay [0.70, 0.52] after ReLU because both are positive. If another unit produced -0.40, ReLU would output 0. That zero says this feature is inactive for the current example.

blocks.title: Activation role
blocks.prompt: Why add nonlinear activations between layers?

options.text: To make the train/test split random.
To let the network represent curved or piecewise decision boundaries.
To remove the need for a loss function.

blocks.explanation: Activations give the network expressive power beyond one linear map.

modules.title: Forward pass computes prediction and loss
modules.sub: Training begins by running data through the current network.
modules.summary: The forward pass produces the prediction that the loss will judge.
objectives: Trace hidden activations into an output score.
Connect output score to a task loss.
Separate forward computation from parameter update.

blocks.title: The forward pass creates the error signal

spans.text: After hidden activations, the output layer combines them into a score, such as probability that the ticket is urgent. The loss compares that prediction with the target label. Backpropagation has nothing to send backward until the forward pass creates this loss.

modules.title: Backprop sends blame through the graph
modules.sub: The chain rule turns output error into gradients for each weight.
objectives: Explain backpropagation without memorizing calculus notation.
Verify generated backprop code for update order.

blocks.title: Tiny network-style forward and backward pass
blocks.code:
# One hidden ReLU unit and one output weight for a single example.
x = 2.0
target = 1.0
w1 = 0.4   # input -> hidden
w2 = 0.6   # hidden -> output
lr = 0.1

hidden_pre = w1 * x
hidden = max(0.0, hidden_pre)  # ReLU
pred = w2 * hidden
loss = (pred - target) ** 2

# Backward pass by hand.
dloss_dpred = 2 * (pred - target)
dpred_dw2 = hidden
dpred_dhidden = w2
dhidden_dpre = 1.0 if hidden_pre > 0 else 0.0
dpre_dw1 = x

grad_w2 = dloss_dpred * dpred_dw2
grad_w1 = dloss_dpred * dpred_dhidden * dhidden_dpre * dpre_dw1

w1 = w1 - lr * grad_w1
w2 = w2 - lr * grad_w2

print(round(loss, 4), round(grad_w1, 4), round(grad_w2, 4), round(w1, 4), round(w2, 4))

spans.text: This hand calculation is the chain rule in miniature. Autodiff libraries record the graph and compute these products for many tensors at once.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Predict whether w2 increases or decreases. The prediction starts below target.
predictThenReveal.answer: w2 increases. The prediction is too low, so dloss_dpred is negative, grad_w2 is negative, and subtracting a negative gradient raises w2.

spans.text: Checklist: the explanation includes a forward pass, a loss, chain-rule gradients, an optimizer update, and a validation check; it does not claim backprop stores examples; and it mentions common failures such as vanishing/exploding gradients or bad learning rates.

modules.title: Optimizers update weights while validation checks generalization
modules.sub: Training progress is not the same as real-world readiness.
modules.summary: The optimizer follows gradients; validation asks whether learning transfers.
objectives: Name overfitting, leakage, and objective mismatch as failures.
Use validation loss to decide when to stop or change design.

spans.text: An optimizer such as stochastic gradient descent or Adam uses gradients to update weights across many batches. If the training loss falls, the network is fitting the training signal. But validation data asks a different question: does the learned pattern work on examples not used for updates?
Failure modes include overfitting, data leakage, vanishing or exploding gradients, bad learning rates, objective mismatch, dataset bias, and catastrophic forgetting during fine-tuning.

blocks.ruleOfThumb: Trust a training run only when optimization and validation tell a coherent story.
blocks.useWhen: Use neural networks when learned representations help with language, perception, generation, ranking, or noisy pattern recognition.
blocks.avoidWhen: Prefer simpler models or rules when the task is small, highly regulated, or needs strong interpretability.

blocks.title: Training vs validation
blocks.prompt: What does falling training loss with rising validation loss suggest?

options.text: The network may be overfitting or the evaluation split may be compromised.
The model has definitely become production-ready.
